description: Inspiring the next gen of astronauts.
summary:
We built Junior Astronaut Trainer, a free, browser-based 3D simulation in English and Arabic that puts young explorers in the boots of a Moon or Mars cadet.

Instead of reading textbooks or taking multiple-choice quizzes, players suit up in real NASA gear—like the Artemis AxEMU or Z-2—and explore 3D lunar and Martian bases under real planetary gravity. Along the way, they inspect actual NASA hardware and face live, animated emergencies like solar flares, freezing lunar shadows, and Martian dust storms. Every choice forces them to balance oxygen, power, and base safety, showing the immediate visual consequences of their decisions.

Supported by an interactive NASA CAPCOM bot that answers space questions with real agency data, our project turns intimidating space engineering into hands-on play. It matters because the kids who will actually walk on Mars are in classrooms right now—and giving them an accessible, fun way to experience real space challenges sparks the curiosity they need to get there.
details:
How It Works Junior Astronaut Trainer is a free, browser-based 3D game where kids train for real missions on the Moon and Mars without needing to download anything. Players choose between the Lunar South Pole or Mars's Jezero Crater, enter their astronaut name, and suit up in real NASA gear like the Artemis AxEMU, Z-2 prototype, or Orion OCSS, each offering realistic trade-offs in oxygen, radiation protection, or agility.

Once on the surface, cadets walk and jump under real lunar or Martian gravity. Exploring the 3D outpost lets them inspect real NASA hardware—like Vertical Solar Arrays, VIPER ice drills, and Perseverance's MOXIE oxygen generator—with real agency photos and facts. Along the way, live emergencies hit the base: solar flares, freezing shadows, and global Martian dust storms. Players make tough calls balancing oxygen, power, and base safety, watching the visual consequences play out in real time. A built-in NASA CAPCOM chat bot is also available anytime to answer space questions using official NASA sources.

Benefits and Intended Impact Kids learn best by doing, not by memorizing textbook facts or taking multiple-choice quizzes. By letting students experience real engineering trade-offs firsthand, we want to spark genuine curiosity in the generation that will actually live and work on the Moon and Mars. Because the game runs smoothly on basic school laptops and tablets, any classroom can use it right away.

Tools and Technologies Used We built the entire experience using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript packaged into a single, fast-loading web file so anyone can play it without installing software. For the 3D worlds, planetary gravity, and weather particles, we used Three.js alongside HTML5 Canvas for live hazard and consequence animations. Everything in the game is grounded in official NASA planetary fact sheets, NASA Space Weather (DONKI) alerts, and real NASA mission photography.

Creativity and What We Considered Instead of showing a boring "wrong answer" screen, we designed every decision to trigger a live visual simulation showing how the base reacts—whether shields deflect a solar storm or unheated pipes freeze over. We also wanted the game to feel welcoming and accessible to students everywhere, so we added instant one-click switching between English and Arabic (with full right-to-left layout support) paired with a familiar blocky avatar style that young players immediately enjoy.
